title: Michelin-Starred Indienne Brings Fine Indian Dining From Chicago to New York's Hudson Yards
excerpt: Chef Sujan Sarkar's celebrated tasting-menu restaurant opens its second location in Manhattan, marking a new chapter for upscale Indian cuisine in America.
body:
When Indienne earned a Michelin star within its first year in Chicago's River North neighborhood, it announced something that had been building quietly across American dining: Indian cuisine could compete at the highest level of fine dining — not by mimicking French techniques, but by deepening its own.

Now, chef Sujan Sarkar is bringing that vision to New York. Indienne opened on May 28 inside Henry Hall at 515 West 38th Street in Hudson Yards, with 34 seats and three nine-course tasting menus that move from chaat-inspired openers through seasonal courses layered with regional Indian spices and textures.

## A Tasting Menu With Deep Indian Roots

The non-vegetarian menu is priced at $195, with vegetarian and vegan options at $175 — price points that place Indienne alongside New York's most ambitious restaurants. But what sets it apart is the unapologetic Indian foundation of every course.

Where many upscale Indian restaurants in America have historically softened their identity to fit Western fine-dining templates, Indienne does the opposite. The progression begins with chaat — the street food tradition that is essentially India's answer to tapas — before building through courses that highlight regional influences from Kerala, Punjab, Bengal, and the Konkan coast.

The wine program is led by Chris Farrell, and a cocktail program focused on sustainability uses ingredients recycled from the kitchen. The interiors, designed in collaboration with MAPA Mueller, blend textured finishes, sculptural lighting, and blush-toned seating with artwork by Chicago-based artist Ken Andjulis, whose paintings draw on the colors and chaos of Holi.

## Why New York, Why Now

New York has long had a complicated relationship with Indian food. The city's Curry Row on East 6th Street once symbolized affordable, often generic Indian dining. But over the past decade, a new wave of restaurants — from Semma's Michelin-starred South Indian cooking to Dhamaka's unapologetic regional flavors — has been rewriting that narrative.

Indienne's arrival adds another dimension. Sarkar is not just opening a restaurant; he is opening alongside two additional concepts planned for Henry Hall, signaling a multi-brand Indian dining presence in one of Manhattan's most prominent developments.

## The Diaspora Angle

For Indian Americans, Indienne represents something beyond a restaurant opening. It is a statement that Indian cuisine belongs in the same conversation as the world's great culinary traditions — not as a novelty, not as fusion, but on its own terms.

The $195 price point will draw skeptics. But Sarkar's Chicago track record suggests that diners who sit through the nine-course journey leave as converts. In a city where a tasting menu at Eleven Madison Park costs $365, Indienne's pricing actually represents a relative value proposition — one that happens to come with flavors most New Yorkers have never experienced at this level of refinement.

## What's Next

Indienne joins a growing roster of Indian fine-dining concepts that are reshaping perceptions across American cities. With the Hudson Yards location, Sarkar is betting that New York is ready for Indian cuisine that doesn't compromise, doesn't explain itself, and doesn't apologize for its ambition. Given the trajectory of the past two years, it's a bet worth watching.
author: Diaspora Desk
